overview: The Kazan Khanate arose in the Middle Volga and Kama region as the Golden Horde fragmented, conventionally dated to 1438 or 1445. Its inhabitants included Turkic and Finno-Ugric communities. The imported 1530 to 1600 outline is seriously misplaced: it excludes Kazan itself and extends towards western Siberia. It should not be treated as the territory of this khanate. The historical state ended in 1552, before the map interval closes.

periods.title: The Kazan Khanate
periods.summary: Its emergence is dated to 1438 or, in an alternative chronology, 1445; conquest ended the independent state.

sections.title: A capital and a royal family

items.text: Kazan’s citadel stood at the centre of the khanate’s political, military and commercial life. Archaeological remains are essential for understanding that capital: much of the Kremlin visible today belongs to construction after the Russian conquest. Its surviving ensemble combines buildings from the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries with evidence of earlier occupation, rather than preserving the khans’ city intact.

When Khan Safa Giray died in 1549, his young son Utyamysh Giray inherited power and his mother Suyumbike became regent. She governed amid rival aristocratic groups and conflict with Moscow. Her government was overthrown in 1551, and mother and son were sent to Moscow. A royal childhood could become a matter of dangerous international politics.

sections.title: Food, work and things people used

items.text: A regional synthesis covering the thirteenth to mid-sixteenth centuries lists rye, oats, barley, millet and buckwheat among farmers’ crops. Different ploughs suited different soils, while harrows broke up the ground and scythes cut vegetation. This was a landscape of cultivated fields as well as rivers and towns; the list describes the broader period rather than the contents of one excavated pantry.

Village households also worked leather and wood, producing goods that included wooden utensils and the timber frames of buildings. Women spun thread and wove cloth; specialist smiths and potters supplied neighbours and markets. Keeping a household going involved a long chain of skilled tasks, well before anyone could sit down to a meal.

Excavations at the Kazan Kremlin and Iske Kazan have recovered wheel-made pottery, including jars, jugs, bowls, plates and inkwells. Some vessels were glazed or decorated with incised patterns. Finds also include pouring vessels with animal-shaped details, such as ram or horse heads. Even a practical container could have a little personality.

Leather shoes could carry embossed patterns or embroidery in silk thread. Archaeologists also found carved alabaster panels with scrolling plant ornament used in buildings. These surviving pieces show makers decorating both things worn on the body and the spaces around them. The evidence records skilled work, although it cannot tell us what every family could afford.

A surviving brass wine pitcher shaped like a waterbird preserves a craftsman’s name: Nasyr, identified as Emin Khan’s coppersmith. It belongs to the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century. A named maker is a welcome change from anonymous objects: we can connect metalworking skill with a particular person, while recognising that this elaborate vessel belonged to a privileged setting.

A charter issued by Sahib Giray in 1523 protected a named family’s privileges. It exempted its beneficiaries from demands such as certain taxes, providing lodgings, and supplying food or fodder. These exemptions reveal the kinds of obligations other people could face. They were special privileges, rather than a promise that every household could turn away officials.

The seal on that 1523 charter includes the Arabic words “السلطان الاعظم”, meaning “The greatest sovereign”. This sample follows the scholarly transcription and translation published by I. A. Mustakimov on page 43 of his edition. It is Arabic in the seal of a Turkic-language document, shown here in modern type rather than as a picture of the original lettering.

The poet Muhammadyar explored what a good society should look like. His Gift to Men, written in 1539 to 1540, praised justice, honesty and peaceful life. Light of Hearts followed in 1542, discussing virtues that rulers and others should practise. These were arguments about how people ought to behave, not a report that everyone already behaved beautifully.

The medrese, or school, attached to Kazan’s principal mosque had a substantial manuscript collection. Across the Tatar khanates, such libraries gathered works in Arabic, Persian and Turkic literary traditions. Books connected religious study with a wider written culture. A school library tells us that organised learning existed, without establishing that every child attended school.

The 1523 charter resurfaced in 1912, long after the khanate had ended. Scholar Saeed Vakhidi found it with a farmer, Rakhmatulla Akhmarov, who kept it as a healing talisman. It entered a museum collection after Vakhidi acquired it in 1920. This later belief helped preserve an important document; it is not evidence that the charter could cure illness.

ending.text: Ivan IV’s forces captured Kazan in October 1552 and ended the independent khanate. Resistance in its former lands continued until 1557. Russian administration replaced the khans’ government, while Tatar language, religious life and cultural traditions continued through major disruption. The imported map endpoint of 1600 does not mark a later fall of this state.
